tldr: By cleverly combining visual-inertial tracking (Basalt) with a Rust-based 3DGS framework (Brush), Stipple achieves high-quality, real-time incremental 3D Gaussian reconstruction from stereo camera and IMU inputs, even running in non-CUDA environments.
hero_caption: Overall system flow of Stipple. Among the keyframes from VIO, only those containing unexplored areas are selected as "anchor frames" for heavy stereo depth estimation and Gaussian initialization. The rest are sent to asynchronous training, balancing high speed and high image quality.
overview:
When robots or XR devices explore unknown environments, obtaining a photorealistic, dense 3D representation on the fly is extremely valuable. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows very fast rendering, conventional pipelines rely on heavy offline SfM pre-processing (such as COLMAP) and lengthy batch optimization. This makes them far too slow for real-time robotic applications.

To solve this, the authors integrated Basalt—a proven, fast visual-inertial odometry (VIO) system—with Brush, a GPU-vendor-agnostic Rust implementation of 3DGS. Instead of performing the biggest computational bottleneck, stereo depth estimation, on every keyframe, the system projects the current map and selectively picks only frames with many unmapped regions (about 10% of all frames) as "anchor frames" to initialize Gaussians. By routing other keyframes solely to standard optimization, they built a fully asynchronous incremental training pipeline that never blocks tracking.

Evaluated on benchmark datasets including EuRoC and the Monado SLAM Dataset, Stipple was compared against PhotoSLAM and CaRtGS, two leading real-time stereo baselines. The results show that Stipple achieves 2 to 3 times faster tracking speeds (over 200 fps) while outperforming them by 1 to 3 dB in rendering quality (PSNR and SSIM) across most sequences.
contributions: Proposed a GPU-vendor-agnostic pipeline that estimates camera trajectories and reconstructs environment maps with 3DGS completely in real time and in parallel using stereo images and IMU data.

Established an efficient Gaussian placement and optimization strategy by restricting heavy stereo depth estimation only to "anchor frames" with many unmapped regions, combined with occupancy grid culling and SSIM-based densification.
Built a synchronization mechanism that quickly applies rigid transformations in bulk to the Gaussians associated with each anchor frame when loop closures occur in the VIO.

Demonstrated performance substantially superior to existing real-time stereo baselines (PhotoSLAM, CaRtGS) on the EuRoC and Monado SLAM datasets, in terms of both frame rate and reconstruction quality.

sections.heading: Clean 3D maps on the fly: Tackling real-time 3DGS
sections.summary: Robotics and XR demand dense, photorealistic 3D reconstruction for immediate interaction with environments, but traditional 3DGS is too computationally heavy for real-time use. This paper presents Stipple, an incremental reconstruction system that leverages VIO tracking information to run in real time without being tied to a specific GPU vendor.
sections.details:
In robotics and augmented reality (XR), reconstructing the surrounding 3D environment in real time directly impacts critical decision-making, such as navigation, manipulation, and remote monitoring for disaster rescue drones. Traditional point cloud-based reconstruction is lightweight but sparse, requiring expensive meshing to recover fine surface photometric details. On the other hand, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offers photorealistic and fast rendering, but requires heavy offline SfM like COLMAP and iterative batch optimization, making on-the-fly real-time reconstruction impossible.

Many robots and XR devices are already equipped with stereo cameras and inertial measurement units (IMUs), running fast ego-motion tracking via Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO). The authors focused on this fact and designed an approach that bypasses heavy preprocessing by feeding camera poses and keyframes generated by VIO directly into the 3DGS training pipeline.

The main contribution of this work is a framework built on a Rust and CubeCL implementation that is not tied to specific hardware (like CUDA), running tracking and Gaussian reconstruction completely in parallel in real time. It incorporates several strategies coordinated with VIO, including stereo depth estimation, keyframe selection, and Gaussian synchronization during loop closures.

captions.F1: Qualitative comparison under identical runtime constraints and hardware. Baseline methods (PhotoSLAM, CaRtGS) exhibit noticeable artifact distortion and needle-like Gaussian noise, while the proposed method (Ours) produces sharp, geometrically consistent reconstructions close to the ground truth (GT).

sections.heading: Fusing 3DGS and SLAM: Existing limitations and Stipple's place
sections.summary: While combining 3DGS with SLAM is popular, most systems require RGB-D cameras and run at only a few frames per second. Even among real-time methods, very few support stereo cameras, and most rely heavily on CUDA. This work bridges that gap with stereo-inertial input and cross-platform support.
sections.details:
Early methods applying 3DGS to SLAM (such as SplaTAM and MonoGS) achieved high rendering quality by representing both maps and tracking with Gaussians alone, but their processing speeds were only a few fps, far from real-time. Systems like RTG-SLAM split opaque surface Gaussians from transparent residual Gaussians to speed up rendering, but still fell short of 20 fps. In addition, most methods require depth sensors (RGB-D) and do not support stereo cameras with IMUs, which is the most practical setup in robotics.

Among systems targeting real-time performance are Photo-SLAM, which combines ORB-SLAM3 with Gaussian representations; CaRtGS, which refines Gaussian optimization; and RGBD GS-ICP SLAM, which utilizes Generalized-ICP. However, only Photo-SLAM and CaRtGS practically support stereo cameras, and both are tightly coupled to NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA).

This work integrates Basalt, a fast and resource-efficient VIO system, with Brush, a GPU-agnostic 3DGS implementation running on WebGPU/Vulkan via CubeCL. It natively handles stereo-inertial inputs without CUDA dependencies, achieving state-of-the-art tracking frame rates and reconstruction quality that surpass existing real-time stereo baselines.

sections.heading: Never block tracking! Anchor frames and efficient training
sections.summary: Tracking and training threads are completely decoupled, running in parallel with mutexes only for GPU access arbitration. Keyframes with large unmapped regions upon map projection are promoted to "anchor frames" for concentrated depth estimation and Gaussian insertion, ensuring real-time performance.
sections.details:
Basalt is used for tracking, processing the incoming stereo-inertial stream. Images are undistorted and stereo-rectified using OpenCV. The core of this method is that the tracking thread is never blocked by mapping or training tasks. The two threads only share a mutex that arbitrates GPU access for depth estimation and optimization.

Running depth estimation on every keyframe would inevitably drop frames. Instead, the system projects the current map and computes the percentage of pixels with alpha (opacity) below 0.05. Only keyframes where this unmapped area exceeds 5% are promoted to "anchor frames." Because anchor frames make up only about 10% of all keyframes, computational overhead is dramatically reduced.

### 3.1 Adding Gaussians
Adding Gaussians for an anchor frame proceeds as follows:
- 1. Depth-based seeding: Metric depth is estimated using FoundationStereo (or lightweight BM/SGBM) and unprojected into a 3D point cloud.
- 2. Occupancy culling: Existing Gaussian centers are hashed into a CPU-side uniform grid (0.1 m cell size), and candidate points in already occupied space are discarded.
- 3. Burst optimization: A short round of optimization runs with a higher learning rate to check if simple planar areas, like walls, can be represented by this initial set of points alone.
- 4. SSIM-based densification: Per-pixel SSIM is computed between the rendered image and the ground truth. New Gaussians are importance-sampled with probability proportional to the error ($1.0 - \text{SSIM}$), adding points precisely where complex structures remain unresolved.
- 5. Convergence training: Additional training runs to blend the newly inserted Gaussians locally.
When no anchor frames are queued, an optimization step runs by picking one keyframe uniformly at random from past keyframes.

### 3.2 Loss Formulation
The overall loss function includes photometric color matching terms $\mathcal{L}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{SSIM}}$, alongside three regularization terms. First is an inverse depth L1 loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{depth}}$ applied only to anchor frames. Second is an anti-needle loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{needle}}$ to prevent Gaussian variances from degenerating into needle-like shapes. Third is a scale regularization term $\mathcal{L}_{\text{scale}}$ to prevent Gaussians from growing excessively large and causing foggy artifacts, as seen in EuRoC.

### 3.3 Loop Closure
When loop closure occurs on the VIO side, all keyframe poses are updated. Because Gaussians are stored contiguously in memory for each anchor frame, the system can apply the rigid transformation (rotation and translation) from the anchor frame directly to the Gaussian centers and covariance matrices, completing the geometric correction almost instantly.

sections.heading: Crushing baselines in speed and quality: Real-world benchmark tests
sections.summary: Evaluations on EuRoC and the Monado SLAM Dataset demonstrate tracking speeds over 200 fps—2 to 3 times faster than PhotoSLAM and CaRtGS—along with superior image quality. However, excessive Gaussian generation was observed in specific environments.
sections.details:
Experiments were run on a workstation equipped with a Ryzen 9 9950X and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB). Input sequences were played at their native frame rates (real-time playback) to ensure fair comparisons without granting any method extra computation time.

### 4.2 & 4.3 Qualitative and Quantitative Results
- EuRoC Vicon Room (Table 1): The proposed method led the baselines across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, beating them by roughly 1 to 3 dB in PSNR. Notably, it recorded a tracking speed of 211 fps, compared to 69–72 fps for the baselines.
- Monado SLAM Dataset (MSD: Tables 3, 4, 5): On this VR headset dataset, the method achieved ultra-fast tracking up to 264 fps. While PhotoSLAM and CaRtGS frequently lost tracking and failed completely (on all MOO sequences and most MGO sequences), Stipple completed every sequence and beat the baselines by 4.3 to 5.4 dB in PSNR on comparable runs.
- EuRoC Machine Hall (Table 2) exception: In the Machine Hall sequences, the method scored an average PSNR of 19.48 dB, trailing CaRtGS (average 21.80 dB). The SSIM densification triggered too aggressively, causing Gaussian counts to explode to an average of 394k (compared to 118k for CaRtGS) and preventing optimization from converging within the time budget.

### 4.4 Ablation Study
In ablation experiments on the EuRoC V1_01 sequence (Table 6), local camera pose refinement during training contributed the most, improving PSNR by +0.84 dB. The maximum scale loss also proved effective at suppressing oversized Gaussians.

sections.heading: Conclusion: VIO and 3DGS synergy drives the future of robot vision
sections.summary: Combining the efficiency of VIO with a GPU-agnostic 3DGS pipeline proves that real-time, high-quality incremental 3D reconstruction is possible. Despite issues with Gaussian over-generation in certain scenes, this is a highly practical step toward immediate environmental understanding for robotics and XR.
sections.details:
This work proposed a pipeline that leverages the fast tracking and loop-correction capabilities of VIO, confining stereo depth estimation strictly to anchor frames to reconstruct unknown environments within seconds without interrupting tracking.

It boasts tracking frame rates 2 to 3 times faster than existing stereo-capable methods and offers the flexibility to run on non-CUDA hardware. While future work remains to address Gaussian count explosions in specific textured environments like Machine Hall, this study highlights the immense potential that the complementary nature of SLAM and 3DGS brings to real-time robotics and XR applications.

takeaways: The key to real-time 3DGS is culling: heavy stereo depth estimation and Gaussian generation should not run every frame, but only on "anchor frames" that reveal unmapped areas upon map projection.
Decoupling the VIO tracking thread from the 3DGS training thread with minimal GPU mutex synchronization allows tracking speeds to exceed 200 fps.
When loop closures occur, storing Gaussians contiguously by anchor frame enables instantaneous global geometric alignment through bulk rigid body transformations.
Incorporating local camera pose refinement into the 3DGS optimization loop provides the largest boost to reconstruction image quality.
limitations: In certain environments like EuRoC Machine Hall, SSIM-based densification triggers excessively, causing Gaussian counts to explode and preventing optimization from converging within real-time budgets, which degrades image quality.
Evaluations are performed on each method's own keyframes, meaning viewpoints differ across methods; rigorous holdout evaluation using identical test poses remains an area for future work.
In multi-camera setups like a 4-camera VR headset, side cameras are only used for VIO tracking and are not yet utilized for Gaussian reconstruction.
